summary:
LUNAR/NAV was designed as an interactive 6-part application. This allows you to plan out your lunar mission.

From choosing your landing site, to assessing potential hazards within the landscape, you can create a customisable landing ellipse. We have also modelled trajectories from Earth to Moon, calculated spacecraft fuel needs, tracked power generation and usage, and calculated communication reliability based on the visibility of the sun and Earth. Finally we also have a 3D interactive mission where you can explore the surface of the moon with a rover, avoiding hazards, gathering samples and returning to base.

All 6 systems are connected, meaning when you change your landing coordinates, spacecraft or mission time, connected analysis will update. This means you can see how one choice will affect the whole mission.

By using NASA resources, astronomical calculations and interactive simulations we’ve made it easy to understand complex aerospace engineering concepts. This application helps you identify if your lunar mission is feasible and compare different landing sites.
details:
The Problem:

We need to find areas of flat land to land on the moon. We must ensure that the spacecraft can get enough light to power it and also communicate with Earth. This can be challenging at the South Pole due to the Sun always being low on the horizon.

The Solution:

LUNAR/NAV is an interactive mission planning website. It contains 6 connected modules:

Site & Light: Allows users to view the surface of the moon and choose specific coordinates. They can view a customisable ellipse and see how much sun and earth there are in relation to the horizon. You can upload NASA LOLA data to see how much light is blocked by surrounding terrain.

Mission Transfer: Choose the type of spacecraft used, launch site and launch date. The interactive heliocentric and geocentric visualisations show how the mission progresses. Basic orbit calculations are used to give an estimate of what is required and how much fuel is needed.

Energy: Gives an estimate of how much energy will be produced, used and in battery depending on the type of spacecraft. The amount of energy produced will vary depending on how much sun there is.

Communications: Shows how much line of sight there is to Earth, how long the signal takes and any communication issues. It shows how a relay system would work for missions on the far side of the moon.

Lunar Surface Expedition: An interactive 3D simulation that shows how the rover moves in lunar gravity, how it navigates around obstacles, how it manages its power and how it collects samples. The user travels to a cave, collects a rock sample and returns it to their research base.

Mission Comparisons: Compare different landing sites on different dates. Calculates how much light there will be, how much line of sight to Earth and how much overlap there is. It also calculates the most amount of continuous darkness and communication blackouts.

Technical:

The website was created using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG, Canvas and WebGL 2. Preprocessing tools were written in Python to handle NASA lunar elevation data using NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio and PyProj.

An astronomical ephemeris was included to provide the geometry of the moon’s sky depending on the date. Physical constants, orbital references, images of the moon and sources of terrain data were provided by NASA/JPL.

Creativity:

LUNAR/NAV provides a single place to plan many aspects of a lunar mission. The mission timer can be seen so users can see how timing affects different systems.

This project was a great way to bring together visualising, calculations, comparisons and game play. It makes lunar exploration easy to understand for students and a good foundation for mission planning discussions.

Scientific Limitations:

This is an interactive scientific application, it is not a certified flight planning tool. The orbits, some spacecraft details and the rover terrain have been simplified. The local mountains blocking have been predicted using NASA elevation data for the chosen location.

AI Support:

ChatGPT by OpenAI helped with developing the software, designing the interface, and debugging.
